Lighten
līt´'n
v. (to illuminate; to make less heavy; rendering Hebrew or, nagah, and qalal, Greek photizo and apokalupsis)
Two English words of different descent share the form: from light the illumination, and from light the opposite of heavy. The Authorized Version uses both.

Biblical Definition

Simeon's song: “A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel” (Luk 2:32). David: “lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” (Psa 13:3); “the LORD will lighten my darkness” (2Sa 22:29). The city that needs no sun: “the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof” (Rev 21:23). Ezra: God has given a little reviving, “to lighten our eyes” (Ezr 9:8). In the other sense, Jonah's sailors “cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them” (Jon 1:5), and the Philistine priests hoped God would “lighten his hand from off you” (1Sa 6:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines lighten as to illuminate, to fill with light; and, as a second word, to make lighter, to reduce in weight, to alleviate.

expand to see more

LIGHTEN, v.t. To dissipate darkness; to fill with light; to spread over with light; to illuminate.

2. To illuminate with knowledge.

LIGHTEN, v.t. To make lighter; to reduce in weight; to make less heavy.

2. To alleviate; to make less burdensome or afflictive.

Key Scripture

Luk 2:32 — "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel."

Psa 13:3 — "Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;"

Rev 21:23 — "And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof."

Jon 1:5 — "Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep."

2Sa 22:29 — "For thou art my lamp, O LORD: and the LORD will lighten my darkness."

1Sa 6:5 — "Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land."

Modern Corruption

Ministries lighten the load by throwing the cargo overboard, and the only lightening Scripture praises is the light in the eyes.

expand to see more

Jonah's sailors lightened the ship by casting the wares into the sea, and it did nothing, because the weight was a sleeping prophet in the hold. The church has its own version of the manoeuvre: when the storm comes, throw doctrine overboard — the hard sayings, the hell, the wrath, the exclusivity of Christ — and the ship rides no higher, because the weight was never the cargo. The other lightening is what Scripture asks for: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death; a light to lighten the Gentiles. Simeon's Greek is apokalupsis, a revelation — the child in his arms was light for the unveiling of the nations, and the city at the end has no sun because the glory of God lightens it. Lightening in the Bible is something done to eyes, not to loads.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew or (H215), to give light; nagah (H5050), to shine; qalal (H7043), to make light, lessen; Greek photizo (G5461), to illuminate; apokalupsis (G602), an unveiling.

expand to see more

Hebrew or, hiphil (H215) — to give light, lighten; Psalm 13:3, Ezra 9:8; nagah (H5050), 2 Samuel 22:29.

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to lighten, make light; 1 Samuel 6:5, Jonah 1:5.

Greek photizo (G5461) — to illuminate; Revelation 21:23; apokalupsis (G602), revelation; Luke 2:32, “to lighten the Gentiles.”

Usage

"“A light to lighten the Gentiles” — Simeon's revelation."

"“Lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” — David's prayer."

"“Cast forth the wares… to lighten it of them” — the cargo overboard, the weight still in the hold."
